Dear students,

Goodluck for the final exam! Here are some logistics announcements:

1. Location: 

182 Students with last names starting from A-R: Hearst Field Annex A1

182 Students with last names starting from S-Z: Evans 10

All 282A Students: Evans 10

2. Time: Wednesday, Dec 17th. 8 AM - 11 AM. 

Please set multiple alarms. Ask a friend to call you in the morning. Don't stay up all night studying and don't oversleep! Eat some breakfast before you come in.

Be there shortly ahead of time so you can find a seat (you'll be asked to sit alternating with empty seats to your sides) and can complete the front page which will involve a distributed identity check. 

3. What to bring: Student ID, Pencils,  water bottle, small non-noisy non-messy snack (e.g. soft granola bar).

No Cheat Sheet is allowed. There will be space for scratch work within the exam printout. (34 pages total including cover page in the front and the doodle page on the back)

And obviously, no electronic devices of any kind. No headphones, no earplugs, nothing. 

The exam will allow no questions and no clarifications --- we have tried to make things unambiguous, and have added optional footnotes for some questions/clarifications that we suspect some students might ask for (but it's completely fine/normal to not have these questions too), but your basic approach on the exam should be to write down what you think the reasonable interpretation is if you have any confusion and just keep going. Any actual ambiguity (in what the exam says in the context of what was taught in the course) that has slipped through our debugging process will be addressed by us fairly during grading. Your focus should only be on doing the exam in front of you.  

Let us know if you have any further questions and goodluck! The best way to study is to understand the homework and the discussion problems. Do get sleep both tonight and tomorrow night, it will help you! A three hour exam is long and the material requires focus. 

Good luck!

182/282A Course Staff.

For those who want more information: (consider this more of a comfort blanket than anything actually useful --- I am posting this to preempt students asking these questions and unfortunately staying up late. You don't have to read this --- sleep has far better return-on-investment.)

The format is very close to the past exams we released. Given 3 hours, there is no way for us to hit everything. So it's quite possible for your favorite topic to not be on the exam --- or to be on it far less than you might prefer. In the same way, it is quite possible that your least favorite topic will be on the exam far more than you prefer. We promise the following major topics will be hit in some way: Optimizers&muP, CNNs and basic architectural building blocks, GNNs, Transformers, RNNs&State-space models, VAEs & Diffusion, and Finetuning.  In addition, you'll have to debug something. There will be math to do, including vector calculus. There will be stuff on the exam that doesn't neatly fit into the above "major topics" categories. If all that sounds completely uninformative to you because all I did was tell you what the class has been about, that's exactly what you should be expecting for a final exam anyway.  

There will be problems that are close to (or even identical to) things you saw in lecture, in discussion, and in homework --- sometimes even hitting things that appeared in exactly one of those places but not the others. There will be other problems that are hitting things that were covered repeatedly in two or three of those places. There will also be problems that leverage the ideas and concepts that you have learned, but ask you to push them in new directions. 

What does any of this tell you practically? Nothing new. We already told you how to study.

So here is something mildly practical: there are more points on the exam than we expect students to be able to do within 3 hours. Why? Because we know that an exam can be stressful and sometimes a problem just makes you draw a blank in the moment. This way, you can comfortably just skip and keep working instead of staying stuck in one place. You can come back later when you've exhausted earning points on things that you know you understand. We have tried to make the exam so that it isn't about exam-taking strategy, it is just about you showing what you understand to the best of your ability. We want people to show us that they know and have internalized the material --- we're not trying to trip you up.
